blocks.text: By the term fundamental particle we mean a particle that has no internal structure, which means it is indivisible. Presently the fundamental constituents of matter are considered to be quarks (protons, neutrons and mesons are made up of quarks) and leptons (including electrons, positrons and neutrinos). They are considered the basic building blocks of matter.

When a nucleus is smashed in an ultra-high-energy particle accelerator, or two high-energy particles collide, entirely new types of particles are created which apparently do not exist within the atoms of ordinary matter; they are the outcome of the violent collisions needed to probe the basic structure of matter. More than a hundred new particles have been identified and classified into families with similar properties. Many were accounted for by the schemes of theoretical physicists, while the rest were named 'strange particles'. They are always created in pairs; for example, when a pion (pi-) collides with a proton, two strange particles, K0 and Lambda0, are created: pi- + p -> K0 + Lambda0.

All particles spin on their axes, and the spin of charged particles makes them tiny magnets. The characteristic spin of electrons, protons and neutrons is 1/2, that of the photon is 1, and that of pions is zero. Half-spin particles obey Pauli's exclusion principle, which says that only one particle of a kind can occupy a given quantum state; these particles are called fermions. Particles with zero or whole-number spin do not obey this principle; they are called bosons, as they obey Bose-Einstein statistics. Further major classifications are:

items: The nucleons and the heavier particles such as Lambda0 and K0 which decay to nucleons are called baryons (heavy).
The muons do not interact strongly with nucleons and are called leptons (small), along with the electron, the tau and the neutrinos.

blocks.text: Both kinds of beta decay (beta-minus and beta-plus) provide evidence that protons and neutrons are not fundamental particles. By the 1960s many new types of particles similar to the neutron and proton had been discovered, as well as many 'midsized' particles called mesons, whose masses were mostly less than nucleon masses but more than the electron mass (other mesons, found later, have masses greater than nucleons). The strongly interacting ones are called pi mesons, or pions, while the weakly interacting particles were named mu mesons, or muons (muons are now classed as leptons). This led to the conclusion that these particles could not be fundamental, and must be made of even smaller constituents, which were named quarks.

Particles can also be classified by the four fundamental forces that act on them. Gravity affects all particles, but its impact at the subatomic level is so small that it is generally disregarded; the electromagnetic force, acting on all charged particles, is well understood and can be considered when necessary. Particles can be broadly classified by whether they interact via the strong force: those that experience the strong force are hadrons, and those that do not are leptons. Examples of hadrons are protons, neutrons and pions, whereas electrons and neutrinos are leptons.

Hadrons are composite subatomic particles that fall into two broad categories: some are bosons, called mesons, such as the pion, while others are fermions, called baryons, with protons and neutrons the key examples. Baryons are made of an odd number of quarks (usually three), and mesons of an even number (usually two: one quark and one antiquark). Leptons interact only through the weak or electromagnetic interactions. No experiment has yet revealed any internal structure for leptons; they appear to be truly fundamental particles that cannot be split. All known leptons have spin 1/2, so all are fermions. The six known leptons are grouped as three pairs (Table 12.3); each pair includes a charged particle (e-, mu-, tau-), its associated neutrino, and the corresponding antiparticles. Charged leptons can combine with other particles to form composite particles such as atoms and positronium, while neutrinos rarely interact with anything and so are rarely observed. The best-known lepton is the electron.

blocks.long_description: Particles that feel the strong force are hadrons, which are either baryons made of three quarks, such as the proton and neutron, or mesons made of a quark and an antiquark, such as pions; particles that do not are leptons, the electron, muon and tau and their neutrinos, which show no inner structure. Six quarks are known, up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom, with charges of plus two thirds or minus one third: two ups and a down give the proton a charge of plus one, and one up and two downs leave the neutron neutral. Forces are carried by bosons, photons, gluons and the W and Z, and the Higgs boson explains how particles get mass. Together these make up the Standard Model, which still cannot explain gravity, dark matter or dark energy.
